# gitlabcommits_files (Resource)

This resource manages a set of files on one branch of one GitLab project. Each create, update or destroy makes a maximum of one commit with all the file changes.

## Example Usage

```terraform
# This resource manages four files on the main branch of platform/gitops.
resource "gitlabcommits_files" "service" {
  project_id     = "platform/gitops"
  branch         = "main"
  commit_message = "chore(frontend): sync gitops manifests via terraform"

  author_name  = "terraform-bot"
  author_email = "terraform@example.com"

  files = {
    "services/frontend/values/dev.yaml" = {
      content = yamlencode({
        replicas = 1
        image    = { tag = "1.2.3" }
      })
    }

    "services/frontend/values/prod.yaml" = {
      content = yamlencode({
        replicas = 5
        image    = { tag = "1.2.3" }
      })
    }

    "services/frontend/argocd/dev.yaml" = {
      content = yamlencode({
        apiVersion = "argoproj.io/v1alpha1"
        kind       = "Application"
        metadata   = { name = "frontend-dev", namespace = "argocd" }
      })
    }

    "scripts/run.sh" = {
      content          = "#!/bin/sh\nexec /app\n"
      execute_filemode = true
    }
  }
}
```

## How the resource works

An operation with no file change makes no commit.
A replacement is a destroy and a create, so it can make two commits in one apply (see [Replacement](#replacement)).
For Git LFS files and for text in an encoding other than UTF-8, see [Limits](../index.md#limits).

### Create

With `adopt_existing = true` (default), the provider reads each path before the commit:

- No file at the path: the commit creates the file.
- The same bytes and the same executable bit: no action. The resource adopts the file.
- Different bytes or a different executable bit: the commit changes only what is different.
- A directory at the path: the apply fails (see [A new path cannot replace a directory](#a-new-path-cannot-replace-a-directory)).

With `adopt_existing = false`, the provider does not read existing files.
If a path already holds a file, GitLab does not accept the commit, and the apply fails.

When the branch does not exist, the create starts it from `create_branch_from`.
In a repository with no commits, a resource without `create_branch_from` makes the first commit, and this commit creates the branch.
If another resource in the same apply commits to the source branch, add `depends_on` on that resource.
Then the new branch gets that commit.

### Refresh

With `detect_drift = true` (default), each refresh reads each file in state from GitLab:

- The refresh records an external change to the content or to the executable bit in state. The next plan shows the change that writes your configuration back. To keep the external change, put the same content and executable bit in the configuration.
- If a file does not exist on the branch, the refresh removes it from state, and the next apply creates it again.
- If the branch and all the files do not exist, the refresh removes the resource from state (see [A branch deleted outside Terraform](#a-branch-deleted-outside-terraform)).

If a file that you manage through `content` changes to bytes that `content` cannot hold, the refresh records them in `content_base64` with a warning.

With `detect_drift = false`, a refresh sends no request (see [Values from the last apply](#values-from-the-last-apply)).

### Update

The update compares the configuration with state, and puts all the actions in one commit:

- A path that you remove from `files`: the commit deletes the file.
- A new path in `files`: the provider uses the rules of [Create](#create).
- Changed content or a changed `execute_filemode`: the commit writes the change.

The delete actions come first in the commit.
So in one apply, a file can become a directory, and a directory of managed files can become a file.
The provider compares bytes, so a change from `content` to `content_base64` with the same bytes gives no action.
A change only to arguments other than `files`, `project_id` and `branch` makes no commit.

### Destroy

A destroy occurs when you run `terraform destroy`, when you remove the resource from the configuration, and in a replacement.
It uses the values in state (see [Values from the last apply](#values-from-the-last-apply)):

- With `delete_on_destroy = true` (default), the destroy makes one commit that deletes all the managed files that still exist. If no managed file exists, it makes no commit.
- With `delete_on_destroy = false`, the destroy only removes the resource from state, and the files stay on the branch.

The destroy never deletes the branch.
With `optimistic_lock = true`, an external change to a file can make the destroy fail, and then it deletes no file (see [Optimistic locking](#optimistic-locking)).

## Caveats

### Many resources on one branch

The provider sends the commits of different resources to one branch one at a time, but only if the resources:

- Use the same provider configuration. Each provider block, an alias included, runs in a separate process.
- Write `project_id` the same way. A numeric ID and a full path for the same project are different values.

Other writers, for example another pipeline or a manual `git push`, are not in this order.
If they commit at the same time as the provider, the apply can fail with "Branch changed while the commit was being created".

Do not put one path in two resources.
Each resource can then overwrite the changes of the other.

### A file that moves to another resource

In one apply, a resource can delete a path that another resource on the same branch and project creates or adopts.
This occurs when:

- You move a path from the `files` of one resource to the `files` of another resource.
- You change a resource address without a `moved` block.
- A `create_before_destroy` replacement keeps the same branch and project.

The resource that had the path then does not delete the file, and gives the warning "File left in place for another resource".
If the delete commit comes first, the file does not exist until the other resource creates it again.
This protection works only in one apply of one provider configuration.

To move a file to another resource:

1. Remove the path from `files` of the old resource.
2. Add the path to `files` of the new resource. Make sure that it has `adopt_existing = true` (default).
3. Make sure that the two resources write `project_id` the same way.
4. Apply the two changes in one `terraform apply`.

Do not do steps 1 and 2 in different applies.
If you remove the path first, that apply deletes the file, and the later apply creates it again.
If you add the path first, the later apply deletes the file.
A third apply creates it again only when the state of the new resource records `detect_drift = true`.

### Replacement

These changes replace the resource:

- A new value of `project_id` or `branch`, or a different spelling of the same project, for example a numeric ID instead of the full path.
- A `project_id` or `branch` value that Terraform does not know at plan time. Keep these values known.
- `terraform apply -replace`, `terraform taint` and `replace_triggered_by`.

By default, Terraform destroys the old object first.
With `delete_on_destroy = true`, the delete commit comes first, and the create commit comes second.
On the same branch, the files do not exist between the two commits.
A pipeline or an Argo CD sync with prune can act on this.
If the new branch does not exist and the resource has no `create_branch_from`, the create fails after the delete commit.

With `create_before_destroy`, Terraform creates the new object first.
On the same branch and project, the new object adopts the files, and the destroy of the old object keeps them.

To keep the files and make no delete commit:

1. Set `delete_on_destroy = false`. Do not change other attributes.
2. Run `terraform apply`. This apply makes no commit.
3. Make the change that replaces the resource.
4. Run `terraform apply`.

Instead of steps 1 and 2, you can remove the old object from state with `terraform state rm <address>`.
A `removed` block with `destroy = false` (Terraform 1.7 and later) also does this, if the configuration no longer declares the address.
On another branch or project, the old files then stay, and no resource manages them.
On the same branch and project, the new object adopts them, with no commit if they already match.

Adoption needs `adopt_existing = true` (default).
With `adopt_existing = false`, the create fails on the existing files.
To change only the address of a resource, use a `moved` block: Terraform then plans no replacement.

### Values from the last apply

Terraform gives a destroy only the state, not the configuration.
So a destroy uses `delete_on_destroy`, `optimistic_lock`, `commit_message`, `author_name` and `author_email` from the last successful apply, also in a replacement.
To change one of these values before a destroy, change it in the configuration.
Then run `terraform apply`. If nothing else changes, this apply makes no commit.

A refresh also gets only the state, so it uses `detect_drift` from the last successful apply.
A failed apply keeps the old value.
With `detect_drift = false` in state:

- A refresh sends no request, and `terraform apply -refresh-only` changes nothing.
- The plan does not show external changes to managed files.
- With `optimistic_lock = true`, an update, chmod or delete of a file that someone changed fails on each apply and destroy.
- A file that someone deleted stays in state. An apply or a destroy skips its delete.

To start refreshes again:

1. Set `detect_drift = true`. Make `files` the same as in the last successful apply.
2. Run `terraform apply`. This apply makes no commit.
3. Put your change back into `files`.
4. Run `terraform plan`.
5. Examine the plan before you apply it.

Do not skip step 3.
If `files` stays the same as in the last successful apply, the next apply overwrites all the changes to the managed files.
This includes a commit of yours that GitLab accepted.

### A branch deleted outside Terraform

Someone can delete the branch outside Terraform, for example with a merge request that deletes its source branch.
With `detect_drift = true` in state, the refresh removes the resource from state with the warning "Branch no longer exists".
The next apply creates the resource again from `create_branch_from`.
Without `create_branch_from`, this apply fails.
With `adopt_existing = true` (default), it makes no commit if the files already match, for example after a merge.

With `detect_drift = false` in state, the resource stays in state.
Then an apply that changes files fails, and the error gives the steps to recover.

### Optimistic locking

With `optimistic_lock = true` (default), update, delete and chmod actions send the `last_commit_id` of the file, except in the first commit of a new branch.
If the file changed after state recorded this value, GitLab does not accept the commit.
The apply then fails with "Concurrent modification detected (optimistic_lock)", and the provider commits nothing.
The error gives the steps to continue.

The value comes from the last refresh or apply, so the lock protects only the time after that point:

- With `detect_drift = true`, the refresh records an external change before the plan. The plan shows the change that writes your content back, and the apply overwrites the external change.
- An apply of a saved plan (`terraform plan -out`) uses the values from the refresh of the plan. If a file that the plan changes gets an external change after that refresh, the apply fails.
- For a path that the apply adopts, the value comes from a read during the apply. The plan does not show the content that the apply overwrites.

The lock checks only the files that the commit changes.
Examine the plan before you apply it.
With `detect_drift = true` and `-auto-approve`, the apply overwrites external changes from before the refresh without an error.

With `optimistic_lock = false`, an update overwrites an external change without a warning.
Before a delete or chmod action, the provider then checks that the path holds a file.

### A new path cannot replace a directory

GitLab lets a new file take the place of a directory, and then deletes the directory with all its content.
To prevent this, the provider checks each path that a commit creates, also with `adopt_existing = false`.
If the path holds a directory, the apply fails with "A directory is in the way", and the provider commits nothing.
An update can create a file at the path of a directory only when the same commit deletes every file in that directory.

The check occurs a short time before the commit.
A writer outside this provider configuration can add a directory at the path during that time, and GitLab then deletes it.
A GitLab error can also hide a directory (see [Limits](../index.md#limits)).

### File content in state

State holds the full content of each managed file as plain text.
This includes content from other writers that a refresh finds.
The provider does not mark `content` and `content_base64` as sensitive, so plan output, apply output and CI logs show them.

Do not put secrets in managed files.
Keep the secrets in a secret store. Refer to them from the file.
Use a state backend that controls access and encrypts the data.
Do not commit large binary files through this provider.

## Schema

### Required

- `branch` (String) The name of the target branch. It must exist, unless you set create_branch_from or the repository has no commits. A new value replaces the resource (see Caveats, Replacement).
- `commit_message` (String) The message of each commit that the resource makes. A destroy commit uses the value in state (see Caveats, Values from the last apply).
- `files` (Attributes Map) The files that the resource manages, as a map from each path in the repository to its file. Terraform changes each path to Unicode NFC, so the provider cannot manage a path in another form (see the provider page, Limits). (see [below for nested schema](#nestedatt--files))
- `project_id` (String) The numeric ID or the full path of the GitLab project, for example group/subgroup/project, without URL encoding. Write it the same way in all resources on one branch. A new value or a different spelling replaces the resource (see Caveats, Replacement).

### Optional

- `adopt_existing` (Boolean) If true (default), the resource adopts a file that already exists at a new path, and changes only the differences from the configuration. If false, a new path that already holds a file makes the apply fail, also after an import.
- `author_email` (String) The email address of the commit author. If you do not set it, GitLab uses its default. A destroy commit uses the value in state.
- `author_name` (String) The name of the commit author. If you do not set it, GitLab uses its default. A destroy commit uses the value in state.
- `create_branch_from` (String) If the target branch does not exist, the create starts it from this branch name or full commit SHA, for example main. A tag name or a short SHA does not work. A later change makes no commit and no replacement.
- `delete_on_destroy` (Boolean) If true (default), a destroy deletes the managed files in a maximum of one commit. If false, a destroy keeps the files, but an apply still deletes a path that you remove from files. A destroy uses the value in state.
- `detect_drift` (Boolean) If true (default), each refresh reads the managed files and records external changes in state. If false, a refresh sends no request. A refresh uses the value in state, not the configured value (see Caveats, Values from the last apply).
- `optimistic_lock` (Boolean) If true (default), update, delete and chmod actions send the last_commit_id of the file, except in the first commit of a new branch. If the file changed after the provider read that value, the apply fails. With detect_drift = true, the apply overwrites changes from before the refresh (see Caveats, Optimistic locking).

### Read-Only

- `commit_sha` (String) The SHA of the last commit that this resource made, not the head of the branch. It is null until the first commit. A plan keeps it known when files has the same paths as state and no entry changes.
- `id` (String) The ID of the resource, in the format project_id::branch.

<a id="nestedatt--files"></a>
### Nested Schema for `files`

Optional:

- `content` (String) The content of the file as text. Set exactly one of content and content_base64. Do not put secrets in it (see Caveats, File content in state). For text that is not in Unicode NFC, use content_base64 (see the provider page, Limits).
- `content_base64` (String) The content of the file as standard base64 text with padding, for example for a binary file. Do not put secrets in it (see Caveats, File content in state).
- `execute_filemode` (Boolean) If true, the file gets the executable bit. The default is false. Set true for each file that must keep the executable bit, also for an adopted file.

Read-Only:

- `blob_id` (String) The git object ID of the file content. A plan shows it as known after apply only for a file that the plan adds or changes.
- `last_commit_id` (String) The SHA of the last commit that changed the file, as the last refresh or apply recorded it. With optimistic_lock = true, the provider sends it with each update, delete and chmod of the file.

## Import

Import a resource with the ID `<project_id>::<branch>`.
Import checks that the branch exists, and records only `project_id`, `branch` and `id`.
It reads no file and makes no commit.
A destroy before the next apply deletes no file.
Write `project_id` and `branch` in the configuration exactly as in the import ID, or the next plan replaces the resource.

The next plan shows an update that adds every configured file.
With `adopt_existing = true` (default), the apply adopts the files (see [Create](#create)), and makes no commit if they already match.
With `adopt_existing = false`, the apply fails if a configured path already holds a file.

```shell
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# The ID is <project_id>::<branch>, with project_id exactly as in the configuration.
# With adopt_existing = true (default), the next apply adopts matching files without a commit.
terraform import 'gitlabcommits_files.service' 'platform/gitops::main'
```
